Will this government be re-elected?

A statistical model trained on the polling record of every completed federal term since 1987 reads the signature of Albanese’s second term, about 16 months in — as at 5 September 2026.

This is the first model read — a dated record begins accumulating at the next fortnightly refresh (19 September 2026).

What this number is

The number above is not a poll of voters and it is not a betting price. It comes from a model that was shown the polling history of every completed federal parliamentary term since 1987 — thirteen terms, nine of which ended in the government’s re-election and four in its defeat — and taught to recognise the signature a term shows part-way through: how the prime minister is rated, whether the prime minister still leads as preferred PM, and how far the vote has faded from the last election result. Read against that record, the signature of Albanese’s second term is the signature of a government that goes on to survive.

The honest part of the answer is the width of the band. Thirteen terms and four defeats is a thin history, so the genuine range runs from an uncomfortable 39 to a comfortable 95 per cent. What the record can say clearly is which company this term keeps: three of the four governments that eventually fell already looked markedly sicker than this one at the same age.

How the model reads this term

Five readings, all knowable from published polling, drive the call.

  • Net PM approval · −19 Voters disapprove of Albanese by a net margin of about 19 points. On its own that is a historically bad level — the four defeated governments all carried numbers like this, and a model that looks only at levels does in fact read this term worse than the typical loser.
  • Preferred-PM lead · +14 Albanese still leads the opposition leader by about 14 points as preferred prime minister. Governments that lose usually lose the leadership question as well as the vote.
  • Primary vote · −6.5 on 2025 Labor’s primary is running about 6.5 points under its election vote — a standard post-election fade, not a collapse, on this record.
  • Two-party preferred · −2.9 on 2025 The government remains narrowly in front on two-party preferred — about 52.3 versus 55.2 at the election, 2.9 points off its election pace.
  • Age of the government · 2nd term This is the 2nd consecutive Labor term. More than any single poll, age sorts the fates: no first-term government on this record has been voted out, and the four that fell were in their second, third, fourth and fifth terms. The Gillard government was ousted at exactly this age.

The blend is the point: bad approval levels, but an ordinary post-election fade, with a live preferred-PM cushion, in a young government. That is why the model lands well short of alarm — the terms that fell looked far sicker than this by the same month.

The column that matters today is month 15 — the yardstick nearest this term’s age of 16.1 months.

The four eventual losers read 91, 91, 29 and 76 per cent there, the nine winners ran from 0 to 63 — and the current term read 23 at that age.

You can score 69 per cent on this table by simply always predicting “returned” — incumbents usually win. Tested honestly, with each term held out in turn and never seen by its judge, the model calls ten of thirteen terms correctly from month six onwards, and eleven by the final pre-election read. History blurs at the extremes: the Hawke government’s famous mid-term scare of 1989–90 read as high as 71 per cent ouster-risk at month 12, and it recovered to win the 1990 election — while the 2016–19 Coalition sat at 32 per cent by its final read and survived.

Where this can go wrong

There are only thirteen terms. Four defeats is a tiny sample, and the final-read accuracy of 85 per cent itself carries about fourteen points of statistical noise either way. Treat every number on this page as a best guess with a range attached — which is why the range, not the median, is the most honest figure here.

It cannot see shocks. The model reads the shape of polling, not events. The 2010–13 minority government’s collapse has no antecedent in the record, and the model never calls it — at any horizon. The 2019–22 term flips depending on exactly when you look: the COVID rally peaks at precisely the fifteen-month yardstick. And 1990 is the one genuine comeback on record — a 71 per cent ouster-read at month 12 that still won.

Waiting buys less than you’d think. Accuracy is a flat 77 per cent from month six to month 24; only the final pre-election read climbs to 85. Governments that are structurally finished are visible early — three of the four losers were already long shots at six months. Everything else stays murky until the campaign.

Winning means seats, not the popular vote. Fates are coded by who formed government. Howard’s 1998 win on 49 per cent of the two-party vote counts as a win — the model is about survival, not vote share. And none of this is a forecast of events between now and the election: it is a reading of history’s signatures, and the election itself remains its own fact.

The model, technically

The headline is the best of four constructions tried in the site’s re-election modelling suite (.build/analysis, committed de5dfa4). The ladder, with how each reads Albanese’s second term:

ConstructionRead on Albanese-2025Leave-one-term-out
15-month levels composite (approval, lead, swings scored against the ousted and survivor centroids)−1.18 — worse than the typical ousted term’s level15% (useless)
15-month declines composite (fade from the term’s own honeymoon)+0.86 — a standard honeymoon fade54%
Ridge logistic on per-term trajectory featuresp(ousted) = 0.31 → predict re-elected85% full-term · 77% live
Snapshot / hazard model — the one abovemedian p(ousted) = 0.22, 10–90% [0.05, 0.61]77% at every band, months 6–24 · 75% at 30 · 85% final

The construction. Each completed term contributes snapshots at ages 6, 12, 15, 18, 24 and 30 months plus a final read three months before its last day — ninety snapshots in all. Each snapshot’s features are trailing-three-month summaries knowable at that age: net PM approval, the preferred-PM lead, the primary-vote and two-party swings against the term’s own election result, the government’s incumbency age in consecutive terms, the fraction of the term elapsed (the current term is assumed to run a full span), and the interaction of primary swing with elapsed fraction — seven features in all. Missing values are median-imputed within the training fold; features are standardised within it; the fit is ridge logistic regression with λ = 1.

The validation. Leave-one-term-out: a term’s snapshots are scored only by a model trained on the other twelve. The baseline “always re-elected” scores 69 per cent. Snapshot-level AUC is 0.77 with Brier score 0.182. The interval comes from a 300-draw cluster bootstrap that resamples whole terms, refits, and re-scores the current term each draw. The live call, verbatim:

p(ousted | profile at 16.1mo) = median 0.22 · 10–90% CI [0.05, 0.61] share of bootstrap draws calling ousted (p ≥ 0.5): 18% features: pmNet −18.9 · ppm +14.5 · primSw −6.5 · tppSw −2.9 · govAge 2 · ageFrac 0.44 (the table’s current-term row shows the in-sample profile read: 0.23)

The cross-check. A deliberately different construction — one ridge logistic per term on first-sixteen-month features — reads p(ousted) = 0.31 — same verdict, well short of alarm. Its best-calibrated variant, adding leadership-spill and minority-government flags, holds the same 85 per cent leave-one-term-out accuracy with AUC 0.89 and Brier 0.134. On thirteen terms the estimator is not the constraint — a diagonal LDA ties the ridge and k-nearest-neighbours collapses — and no capacity beyond logistic earns its keep: adjacent accuracies are statistically indistinguishable (85 per cent carries a 95% Wilson interval of roughly [58%, 96%]).

To reproduce: from the repo root, node .build/analysis/reelect-snapshot-hazard.mjs (the headline — its snapshot age defaults to the canonical 16.2 months and moves via --age=N.N), node .build/analysis/reelect-term-ridge.mjs (the cross-check), plus reelect-15mo-levels.mjs and reelect-15mo-declines.mjs (the composites). Both models emit machine-readable results with --json; this page is regenerated from them by .build/refresh-prediction.mjs on a fortnightly due-date gate, and each refresh is one dated, selectable record above. The analysis scripts read poll data straight from origin/main, so they are immune to working-tree state; the canonical numbers live in .build/analysis/README.md. The analysis’s own closing caution stands: this is historical signature analysis, not a forecast.
